title: Which shortcuts help you find someone?
hook: Random long links reach farthest. Do they help a message find its way?

doesNotKnow: that people can find short paths using only local knowledge only if long links are spread across distance scales (probability ∝ 1/d on a ring)

misconception: Purely random long links are best for finding people, since they reach farthest.
objective: The learner can explain that greedy routing on a ring is fastest when long links are drawn with chance ∝ 1/distance (about 29 steps here, vs 38 for uniform and 213 for 1/distance²), because 1/d links exist at every distance scale.

claims.text: In the stage's model (ring of 2,000, one long link each, 1,000 messages per rule), greedy routing averages 38.3 steps with uniform links, 28.5 with 1/d links and 212.6 with 1/d² links.
claims.source: Demo.tsx runRule(): 5 networks from mulberry32 seeds 1-5 (not chosen; the first five) × 200 source/target pairs per network from mulberry32(100 + seed), the same pairs for every rule. Builder ran the lesson's own code in Node on 2026-10-14: q0 38.32, q1 28.52, q2 212.59. Robustness: drawing pairs from the network's own generator instead gave 37.0, 29.5, 219.2, and seeds 11-15 that way gave 38.9, 30.0, 213.1; the order 1/d < uniform << 1/d² held every time. Long-link distance d in 1..1000 drawn with chance ∝ (people at distance d) × d^-q; the message goes to whichever of the two ring neighbours or the long link is closest to the target. Brief's re-run with another generator: 29.5, 37.8, 219.1. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): VERIFIED. Own independent implementation (fc21/sw.mjs), same model and seeds 1-5 with pairs from mulberry32(100 + seed): 38.32, 28.52, 212.59. Robustness, seeds 11-15: 37.86, 29.04, 203.61; seeds 21-25: 37.88, 29.03, 192.61. Order 1/d < uniform << 1/d^2 holds each time; the stage quotes this model's means only.

claims.text: With no long links the average is about 500 steps.
claims.source: Ring of 2,000: mean ring distance between two different people = (2·(1+…+999) + 1000)/1999 = 1,000,000/1,999 ≈ 500.25, and with ring neighbours only each step moves one place. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): VERIFIED. Own sum over all 1,999 other people: mean ring distance 500.25 = 1,000,000 / 1,999; ring-only routing moves one place per step. Stage 'Ring only 500'.

claims.text: Uniform links are mostly far jumps and almost never near ones, so close to the target they rarely help and the last stretch crawls along the ring.
claims.source: Uniform over the other 1,999 people: 999 of 1,999 (about half) of all links are longer than 500. When the message is within distance D of the target, a uniform link lands closer than D with chance about 2D/2000 per holder, so small D takes many ring steps. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): VERIFIED. Own sum: uniform links longer than 500 have share 999/1999 = 0.4997. The 2D/2000 chance per holder near the target follows. Qualitative sentence supported. | REVISED v2 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): reveal now opens 'Look at your link tallies. Uniform links were 89% far and 1% near, so close to the target they rarely help...' (tally numbers in c7). Unverified. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 24): VERIFIED. Own node run of Demo.tsx cdfFor/build/tallyOf, seed 1: uniform links 15 / 201 / 1,784 of 2,000 (1% / 10% / 89%). Means over 1,000 messages reproduce 38.3 / 28.5 / 212.6. Qualitative sentence supported (pass 21 sums still hold).

claims.text: 1/d² links are almost all near and almost never far.
claims.source: With chance ∝ 1/d² over d = 1..1000 (two people at each distance), about 61% of links have length 1 and under 2% are longer than 31 (node sums, 2026-10-14). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): VERIFIED. Own sums with weights 2/d^2 (1 at d = 1000): length 1 share 0.608, longer than 31 share 0.0187. | REVISED v2 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): reveal now quotes the stage tally: '1/d² links were 95% near and 1% far' (c7). Unverified. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 24): VERIFIED. Same run: 1/d^2 links 1,893 / 97 / 10 of 2,000 = 95% near, 5% middle, 0.5% far (Math.round shows 1%). 'Almost all near, almost never far' holds.

claims.text: Only 1/d links come at every scale (near, middle and far in similar shares), so wherever the message is, some contact can cut the remaining distance a lot.
claims.source: With chance ∝ 1/d each doubling band of distances gets roughly the same share of links (about 10-15% each on a ring of 1,024; see every-scale-equally-likely), so a link that halves the remaining distance D has chance of order 1/log N per holder whatever D is. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): VERIFIED. Own sums on this ring of 2,000: each doubling band of lengths gets 9-13% of 1/d links (0.134, 0.111, 0.101, 0.097, 0.095, 0.094, 0.093, 0.093, 0.093, 0.090); source's '10-15% on a ring of 1,024' is for the sibling lesson. Qualitative sentence supported. | REVISED v2 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): reveal now points at the stage tally: 'Only 1/d links came at every scale (41% · 30% · 29%)'. Unverified. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 24): VERIFIED. Same run: 1/d links 825 / 599 / 576 (41% / 30% / 29%), the only rule with every band above 10%; pass 21 doubling-band shares (9-13% each) still hold.

claims.text: On large networks, Kleinberg proved greedy search is fast only when the exponent matches the dimension: 1 for a ring.
claims.source: Kleinberg (2000), 'Navigation in a small world', Nature 406, and 'The small-world phenomenon: an algorithmic perspective', STOC 2000; Easley and Kleinberg (2010) ch. 20. From the brief; builder has not opened these. Attribution: fact-checker confirms. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): VERIFIED. Kleinberg, 'Navigation in a small world', Nature 406, 845 (2000), doi 10.1038/35022643: citation confirmed by search; result (greedy routing efficient iff the exponent equals the lattice dimension) confirmed via secondary sources in search snippets (Cartozo and De Los Rios 2009, arXiv 0901.4710; course slides). Papers not opened. Easley and Kleinberg ch. 20 'The Small-World Phenomenon', with sections on decentralized search and an advanced section analysing it: confirmed by library-catalog search snippets (book host blocked); matches my own knowledge of the book. 'Proved' is fair: Kleinberg's theorems give polylog delivery at the matching exponent and polynomial lower bounds otherwise.

claims.text: In the stage's first seeded network (mulberry32 seed 1, 2,000 links), the long links by ring distance (near 1-10, middle 11-100, far 101-1,000) are 1% / 10% / 89% for uniform links, 41% / 30% / 29% for 1/d links and 95% / 5% / 1% for 1/d² links.
claims.source: Builder's node check (2026-10-14, scratchpad b5x/nf.mjs, same cdfFor/build code and seed 1 as Demo.tsx): counts 15/201/1784, 825/599/576, 1893/97/10 of 2,000. The band edges are the builder's choice. Shown under the ring as 'Links by length' and quoted in the reveal from the learner's recorded tallies. Unverified. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 24): VERIFIED. Own node replay of the Demo code, seed 1 network only (nets[0]): counts 15/201/1784, 825/599/576, 1893/97/10, rounded 1/10/89, 41/30/29, 95/5/1. Note: 1/d^2 far is 10/2000 = 0.5%, shown as 1% by round-half-up; the three 1/d^2 shares sum to 101%. Band edges are the builder's convention.

recall.question: On a ring, each person has one long link drawn with chance ∝ 1/d^q. Passing a message to whichever contact is closest to the target, which q finds targets fastest?
recall.why: 1/d links come at every distance scale, so a holder anywhere can usually cut the remaining distance; uniform links are almost all far jumps and 1/d² links are almost all short ones.
